title: Adding points on a curve
sub: The chord-and-tangent rule, then the same rule mod a prime.

frames.caption: The elliptic curve y² = x³ − 2x + 2 over the real numbers. Its points can be 'added' to give another point on the curve. Take P and Q.
Draw the line through P and Q. Because the equation is cubic, a line that meets the curve twice meets it a third time (counting tangencies and the point at infinity).

Reflect that third point across the x-axis. The result is P + Q = (0.13, -1.32). This rule makes the points into a group: it is associative, the point at infinity acts as zero, and each point's negative is its mirror image.

Adding a point to itself uses the tangent line instead: 2P = (2.08, -2.62). Repeating this (2P, 4P, 8P, ... plus additions) computes kP for huge k in about log₂ k steps. That scalar multiplication is the core operation of elliptic-curve cryptography.

The same addition rule works with arithmetic mod a prime. Over the field of integers mod 109, y² = x³ + 2x + 4 has 127 points including the point at infinity (grey), within Hasse's bound of 110 ± 2√109. There is no picture of a curve any more: just a scatter of points.
Start from G = (0, 2) and keep adding G: G, 2G, 3G, 4G, 5G. Each step lands somewhere unrelated to the last.
20 multiples in. The path jumps around with no visible pattern.

G visits all 127 points before returning to the point at infinity (the number of points is prime, so every point except infinity generates the whole group). Given G and some Q = kG, finding k means, in effect, retracing this path: the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem. With a 256-bit prime instead of 109, no known classical algorithm does fundamentally better than about 2¹²⁸ steps.
